verses.title: Will inherit the land
verses.heading: The end of evil and the reward of hope
verses.meaning: For the evildoers will be cut off, but those who hope in the LORD will inherit the land. The verse contrasts two outcomes. Evildoers will not last, but those who hope in God will receive an inheritance. In Israel's covenant, the land was God's gift to His people. The promise speaks of God's justice over time, not a guarantee about any modern territory.
verses.context: Proverbs 2:20–22 also contrasts the upright dwelling in the land with the wicked being cut off from it. Much later, Jesus echoes the psalm's inheritance language in Matthew 5:5, and Hebrews 11:14–16 describes faithful people seeking a better, heavenly country. These later passages extend the theme while retaining their own settings.
explore: The apparent success of evildoers has an end. Their power does not define the future.
The land was Israel's covenant gift. The promise points to God's lasting provision.
verses.reflect: What does it mean for you to hope in God's promises rather than in present success?
verses.alt: Peaceful families work fertile fields in a sunlit valley.

verses.title: A little while
verses.heading: The wicked will not be found
verses.meaning: From the long horizon of the poem, the rule of the wicked is temporary rather than permanent. Looking for them and finding no trace pictures the end of their power. The verse encourages patient hope in God's justice rather than anxious imitation of wrongdoing. It does not give a date for relief or deny how long suffering can feel.
verses.context: Isaiah 26:20 urges God's people to hide briefly while judgment passes. Hebrews 10:35–39 later uses similar 'little while' language to encourage endurance while awaiting Christ. Job 20:9 uses the image of a wicked person no longer being seen, but it is spoken by Zophar; his argument must not become a rule for judging every sufferer.
explore: Evil's season is limited in God's sight. The phrase encourages patient hope without setting a date.
The image portrays the end of oppressive power. Its present prominence is not permanent.
verses.reflect: How could remembering that evil is temporary help you face today?
verses.alt: An empty abandoned fortress sits on a windswept hill.

verses.title: The meek will inherit
verses.heading: Humble ones receive the promise
verses.meaning: The meek are the humble who trust God rather than force their way through violence or grasping. Though often overlooked, they receive the poem's promised inheritance and delight in abundant peace and well-being. The promise is wider than material wealth. Jesus later echoes this verse in the Beatitudes, giving the humble a place in His picture of God's kingdom.
verses.context: Jesus echoes this promise in Matthew 5:5: 'Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.' In a distinct narrative setting, Numbers 12:1–5 describes Moses as very humble while he faces criticism. Isaiah 29:17–21 also looks toward the humble rejoicing in the LORD as ruthless oppression ends.
explore: Meekness is humble reliance on God. It can resist wrongdoing without grasping for domination.
The word is shalom, meaning peace and wholeness. It is more than wealth.
verses.reflect: What would meekness look like in your relationships this week?
verses.alt: A humble family tends an orchard beside a peaceful table in a green valley.

verses.title: They scheme
verses.heading: The hostility of the wicked
verses.meaning: The psalm acknowledges deliberate hostility against people who seek to do right. Scheming names planned harm, while gnashing teeth expresses rage and contempt. In the BSB this verse ends with a comma: the sentence continues into verse 13, where the Lord's response follows. The threat is real, but it does not receive the final word.
verses.context: Psalm 35:15–17 pictures hostile mockers gnashing their teeth at the psalmist. Much later, Acts 7:52–56 records Stephen's accusers doing the same as he testifies about Jesus. Psalm 2:1–3 supplies another poetic picture of rulers plotting against the LORD and His Anointed. These comparisons do not identify Psalm 37's unnamed opponents.
explore: The wicked make deliberate plans against the righteous. The psalm honestly names this danger.
The gesture expresses rage. It is contempt toward the righteous.
verses.reflect: Have you faced opposition for doing what is right? How could you respond with trust?
verses.alt: Anonymous figures whisper in shadow while a traveler follows a sunlit path in the distance.
